Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

You know, when I took office nearly eight years ago, I promised that Maine won't wait to take action to protect our state, our people, and our economy from the dangers of extreme weather events caused by pollution and changes to our environment. And I promised that we would fight to preserve this special place that we call home; preserve it for the benefit of our children and grandchildren.

The stakes could not be higher. Look no further than the devastating storms of just a few years ago. Storms that impacted our communities, our people, and our economy—that destroyed a lot of infrastructure across the state.

I've made climate action a cornerstone of my Administration. First, we created the Maine Climate Council, and we issued a groundbreaking climate action plan. And we dedicated millions of federal and state dollars to make that plan a reality.

In 2025, we made the single largest investment in storm recovery by any administration in Maine history, and we created the State Resilience Office to build better, stronger public infrastructure to withstand future storms.

That office manages a partnership of more than 300 communities and has awarded more than $29 million in state and federal funds for projects to prepare local communities for flooding, for storm surge, for rising sea levels, and other climate and weather events that put people's lives and livelihoods at risk.

Recently, I was proud to announce the latest round of funding through that partnership: more than $4.7 million in grants to 72 cities and Tribal Governments, including the towns of Bingham and Madawaska:

  • The Town of Bingham will install high-efficiency heat pumps and a rooftop solar system in order to lower their energy costs at the municipally owned Veterans Building;
  • The Town of Madawaska will use their grant to launch the RIDER Program, a shared e-bike fleet in a rural community that doesn't have public transportation;
  • And the Town of Freedom will use its grant to do an energy audit of its buildings and to plan for a bridge replacement across Hustus Brook.

Through these projects and so many more, we are continuing to address the very real threat of severe weather events for the health of our people, the health of our environment, and the health of our economy.

You know that clean air and clean water know no political party. Our planet is neither Democratic nor Republican. It's the home of all of us, and it is the responsibility of all of us and all governments to preserve it for future generations.

I am proud that over the past nearly eight years, we've made cost-effective heat pumps, weatherization programs, and other things available for Maine people and businesses. We've attracted investments in emerging industries and renewables, and we've created good-paying, green collar jobs. We've reduced our reliance on expensive fossil fuels, and we've mobilized scientists, industry leaders, local and state officials, and young people from all over to act as one to address the effects of climate change.

We won't wait for the next storm or the next disaster. We do care. And as the author Wendell Berry wrote, "We care for this home that is ours. A home that we care for as we care for no other place in the world."

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Sep 16, 2026

The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) is reporting a case of measles in Maine; the first case in the state since five cases were confirmed in February of this year. The Maine CDC confirmed the latest case on September 15, 2026. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (U.S. CDC), as of September 11, there were 3,294 confirmed measles cases reported nationwide in 2026.

The individual is an unvaccinated adult from Somerset County. The Maine CDC is working with the facility where potential exposure occurred and is working with them to inform potentially exposed individuals.

Individuals who were at the following location* during the timeframe listed below were potentially exposed to measles and should take precautions and should watch for symptoms for 21 days after September 12:

Location

Date

Time

MaineGeneral Express Care, Waterville 211 Main Street, Waterville, ME

September 12, 2026

8am-11am

*Subject to change as the investigation continues

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. If one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms of measles include:

  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Runny nose
  • Red, watery eyes
  • Rash that spreads from the head down.

Individuals who develop symptoms should contact their health care provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection. If symptoms are consistent with measles, a health care professional may test to determine a measles infection.

Measles can cause severe sickness including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain swelling), and death. An infected person spreads measles through coughs or sneezes. Once infected, a person is contagious from four days before their rash starts through four days afterwards. The virus remains alive for up to two hours on surfaces and in the air. The period from exposure to onset of symptoms is typically 10 to 14 days, but can be longer.

The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best prevention for measles. Individuals who:   

  • have been potentially exposed should review their vaccine history and watch for symptoms.
  • are not immunized or do not know their measles immunization status should get vaccinated.
  • develop symptoms should contact their health provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection.

Recommendations: 

  • Children – Identify and vaccinate children who are not up to date with their MMR vaccines. All children should receive two doses of MMR vaccine. A health care professional should administer the first dose to children at 12 to 15 months old and the second at 4 to 6 years old.
    • Children 6 to 11 months old who will be traveling internationally or domestically to a region with a known active measles outbreak should receive one dose of MMR vaccine, per the Maine CDC’s expanded recommendations for those traveling to a destination with a known outbreak. This dose is not considered part of the routine two-dose series starting at age 12 months.  
  • Adults – All adults should have proof of immunity to measles. Acceptable proof includes one of the following:
    • written documentation of vaccination
    • laboratory evidence of immunity
    • birth before 1957
    • or laboratory confirmation of disease
    • individuals who received a measles vaccine between 1963 to 1967 are encouraged to speak with their doctor to determine if additional vaccination is needed. Those known to have received an inactivated dose measles vaccine should receive a single dose of MMR. Five percent of people who received measles vaccine between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated vaccine.

For adults with no evidence of immunity to measles, the U.S. CDC recommends one dose of MMR vaccine as soon as possible. Adults who are traveling domestically or internationally to a region known to have an active measles outbreak should receive two doses of the vaccine. Pregnant women should not receive any live virus vaccine during pregnancy, including MMR.

Vaccination Information:

  • Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.
  • The U.S. CDC considers people who received two doses of MMR vaccine as a child protected for life. 
  • Some people exposed to the virus may still get measles even if they got the MMR vaccine. In this case, they are more likely to have a milder illness and are also less likely to spread the disease to other people.

For More Information:

  • The Maine CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.maine.gov/dhhs/measles
  • The U.S. CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.cdc.gov/measles/index.html
  • The Maine Immunization Program webpage: https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/mecdc/infectious-disease/immunization/

items.title: Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week - September 28 through October 4
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, food is one of Maine’s most valuable resources and is essential for the health and nutrition of all our 1.4 million residents; and
WHEREAS
, nearly 40 percent of food produced in Maine is never eaten – over 361,000 tons annually – primarily ending up in landfills where it produces dangerous methane gas which is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide and a major contributor to climate change; and
WHEREAS
, Maine people can save money by preventing wasted food, with the average Maine family spending nearly $3,000 annually on food that is thrown away; and
WHEREAS
, over 80 percent of consumers misunderstand food date labels causing large amounts of perfectly good food to be thrown away in homes, businesses, and even food pantries; and
WHEREAS
, Maine communities can substantially reduce their waste disposal costs by preventing wasted food since food is the single largest municipal solid waste component; and
WHEREAS
, Maine K-12 schools have a special role in educating our next generation to reduce, recover, and recycle the estimated 7 million pounds of school food wasted annually; and
WHEREAS
, we can help our farmers, strengthen our local food systems, and conserve our natural resources – water, air, energy, and land – by valuing Maine food and composting food scraps instead of wasting it as trash;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 4, 2026, as
Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week
and I encourage all Maine people to become aware of the wasted food in our homes, schools and all around us, and to commit to stop throwing food away.
In testimony whereof, I have caused
the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this second day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

Maine Heads to The Big E with Food, Farms, and Makers

September 3, 2026

The Maine Building at the Big E returns for 17 days of Maine food, farms, makers, and traditions, September 18 - October 4

AUGUSTA, Maine (September 3, 2026) - From loaded Maine baked potatoes and lobster rolls to wild blueberry crisp, maple milkshakes, smoked salmon, and wood-fired pizza featuring Maine ingredients, the tastes and traditions of Maine are returning to The Big E this fall.

The State of Maine Building, located on the Avenue of States alongside buildings representing the five other New England states, will welcome visitors throughout the 17-day Eastern States Exposition, September 18 through October 4, 2026, in West Springfield, Massachusetts. Maine Day will be celebrated on Saturday, September 19.

For more than a century, the Maine Building has introduced generations of fairgoers to the people, products, and traditions that make Maine stand apart. The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) owns and operates the building as a showcase for Maine agriculture, food, fisheries, forests, tourism, artisans, and businesses.

"The Big E gives Maine a special opportunity to showcase our food, farms, and agricultural businesses to people from across New England and beyond," said DACF Commissioner Amanda Beal. "Food is one of the most immediate and memorable ways to make that connection. Someone may come into the Maine Building for a baked potato, lobster roll, or a maple or wild blueberry dish, but they leave with a greater appreciation for the farmers, producers, and small businesses behind those products."

The Big E is one of the largest fairs in North America, providing Maine businesses with access to an enormous regional marketplace. For exhibiting producers and makers, the opportunity extends beyond sales during the fair, helping introduce their products to new customers and build awareness that can lead to future visits, online purchases, and other business opportunities.

"We view the Big E as both a marketplace and a long-term opportunity to build awareness of Maine agriculture," said DACF Bureau of Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources Director Craig Lapine. "Many of Maine's farms and food businesses are small businesses, and reaching an audience of this scale is difficult to accomplish individually. By bringing them together in the Maine Building, we can show visitors the robust diversity of what Maine grows, harvests, makes and creates."

Taste Maine at The Big E

Food remains one of the biggest draws at the Maine Building, and the 2026 lineup offers fairgoers plenty of ways to experience Maine.

Longtime favorites include the Maine Potato Board's iconic loaded baked potatoes and Maine lobster rolls. Tree of Life Maple Farm will offer organic Maine maple syrup, maple cream, candy, cotton candy, coffee, and milkshakes, while Valley View Orchard Pies brings fruit pies, whoopie pies, and other baked goods from its Oxford bakery.

Maine aquaculture is also on the menu, with the Maine Aquaculture Association offering smoked salmon while introducing visitors to Maine's growing aquaculture sector and the Maine Oyster Trail.

This year's offerings also highlight collaborations among Maine farms and food businesses.

Fields Fields Blueberries, a woman-owned organic wild blueberry farm in Dresden, will serve its renowned wild blueberry crisp topped with Maine-made Gifford's ice cream.

QP Burger Food Truck will bring together products from multiple Maine businesses in its burgers, hot dogs, and sides, including Fox Family Potato Chips, Raye's Mustard, and Morse's sauerkraut.

Fire & Company Catering will showcase Maine flavors through wood-fired pizza and beverages featuring Maine producers and ingredients.

"These collaborations tell an important story about Maine's food economy," Beal said. "When Maine farms, food producers, and businesses use and promote one another's products, the benefit reaches beyond a single business. Visitors get a great Maine experience while seeing firsthand how interconnected our agricultural and food community can be."

More Than Food

The Maine Building experience extends well beyond the menu.

Visitors can shop for Maine-made wood products, jewelry, personal-care products, artisan goods, and gifts. Dailey Woodworking and Friends will feature work from more than a dozen Maine makers, alongside longtime and returning exhibitors including Ledgeway Farm, MARTINI Jewels, Sider's Woodcrafting, Sunshine Apothecary, and Winter Whimsies.

Short-term exhibitors rotating through the building include Maine authors and makers, Liberty Graphics, Pussums Cat Company, Sweet Monkey Business, and West Maquoit Vinegar Works.

The Maine Flower Collective will greet visitors with a display of Maine-grown dried flowers highlighting the state's flower farmers and florists, while the Maine Forest and Logging Museum will help tell the story of Maine's forestry heritage.

The Maine Office of Tourism will also be on hand, along with the Maine Tourism Association, to help visitors discover Maine destinations and experiences.

"Our goal is to spark a connection with Maine that inspires a visit to our state for culinary experiences," said Maine Office of Tourism Director Carolann Ouellette. "The Maine-made products on exhibit at the Big E all tell a story that is shaped by the landscape and culture of Maine. When fair attendees discover a Maine product, they get to learn about the farm and people behind the product, and that develops a bond that we hope will carry forward in a trip to Maine's farms and food businesses.

AUGUSTA, MAINE -In celebration of Deaf culture and the heritage of AmericanSign Language (ASL), as well as Deaf literature, art and folklore, Governor Janet Mills has issued a proclamation designating the week of Sept. 20-26, 2026, as Deaf Culture Week.

To kick off the week, the Commission for the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened will hold its 35th Annual Tea in Celebration of Deaf Culture Week on Sept. 17, from 2 to 4 p.m. at the Hall of Flags in the State House in Augusta. The event is open to the public.

Clayton Marr III will give the keynote address. Marr grew up in Westbrook and currently lives in Knoxville, Tenn. where he is the student activity coordinator for the Tennessee Schools for the Deaf. He works with Deaf students to support their academic success, personal growth, and independence.

"Maine's Deaf community has enriched our state for generations through its language, culture, traditions and contributions. I've proudly declared September 20-26 as Deaf Culture Week in celebration of that heritage and the Deaf and hard-of-hearing Mainers who make our state a better place," said Governor Mills.

"The Maine Department of Labor is proud to support the Commission for the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened and this 35th annual celebration of Deaf culture. I encourage Maine employers to harness the many skills and experiences of people with disabilities. DOL's Bureau of Rehabilitation Services is ready to assist workers and employers with vocational rehabilitation, training and support," said Commissioner Laura Fortman.

This year, the Commission will present seven awards to eight individuals and organizations that have contributed to Deaf culture in Maine.

Awards and their recipients are:

Promoting American Sign Language, Deaf Culture and Deaf People Award Lisa Penney, Donna Van Horn

Citizenship Youth Award Gavin Phelan

Businesses, organizations, educators, and service providers are encouraged to get involved and shape Maine's annual agricultural gathering

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) is inviting businesses, farms, agricultural organizations, educators, researchers, service providers, and others connected to Maine agriculture, food systems, and natural resources to express interest in participating in the 2027 Maine Agricultural Trades Show, scheduled for January 12-14, 2027.

The annual show brings together Maines agricultural community for three days of exhibits, education, professional development, networking, and conversations about the opportunities and challenges facing agriculture and food systems.

DACF is encouraging both returning participants and organizations that have not previously participated to explore ways to become involved.

Many Ways to Participate

The Agricultural Trades Show offers several ways for businesses and organizations to connect with attendees and contribute to the program, including:

  • Exhibit booths for businesses and organizations offering agricultural services, supplies, tools, equipment, programs, and resources.
  • Conference sessions for workshops, annual meetings, continuing education, research and development updates, and discussions focused on agriculture, food systems, and natural resources.
  • The Maine Stage features approximately 40-minute programs designed for broad audience appeal, including farmer spotlights, demonstrations, interviews, and other presentations.
  • Room rentals for focus groups, competitions, meetings, and other agriculture-focused activities.
  • Sponsorship opportunities supporting show programming, hospitality, audiovisual services, and other activities.
  • The Listening Post, which provides opportunities for volunteer-led business coaching, networking, listening sessions, and other activities.

Organizations with ideas, including those that do not fit neatly into any of these categories, are encouraged to submit their interests and connect with show organizers. Questions may be directed to acfagtradesshow@maine.gov.

New Participants and New Ideas Encouraged

The Agricultural Trades Show serves a diverse agricultural community, and DACF is particularly interested in broadening awareness of opportunities to participate.

Farms and producers, agricultural businesses, commodity organizations, food-system partners, educators, researchers, conservation and natural resource organizations, financial and business service providers, workforce development organizations, and others whose work supports Maine agriculture are encouraged to consider how they could contribute.

The interest form is the first step. Submitting the form allows potential participants to identify the opportunities that interest them and provides show organizers with contact information for follow-up as planning progresses.

The priority deadline is September 23, 2026, for early consideration of exhibit space, conference sessions, and room rentals. Initial selection status notifications are expected by October 1. Interest forms will continue to be accepted and reviewed throughout fall 2026, with waitlist requests accepted until the show.

About the Maine Agricultural Trades Show

The Maine Agricultural Trades Show is an annual gathering of Maines agricultural community hosted by the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. The show connects farmers, producers, businesses, organizations, educators, service providers, and the public through exhibits, educational programming, networking, and opportunities to learn about Maine agriculture and the resources available to support it.

items.title: Updates to the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Definitions and Exclusions
items.content_text: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposes to revise a regulatory definition under the Clean Water Act (CWA) permitting regulations pertaining to discharges in the contiguous zone and ocean. The proposal would revise the regulatory definition of "discharge of a pollutant" to reflect and faithfully implement the statutory exclusion of vessels and other floating craft that add pollutants in the contiguous zone or the ocean from inclusion in the definition of "discharge of a pollutant" or "discharge", and thus, from National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) program requirements. The proposed rulemaking would also make conforming and clarifying changes to the NPDES regulatory exclusion for vessels and other floating craft. The effect of these changes would be that the addition of pollutants by a vessel or other floating craft in the contiguous zone or the ocean that is not secured to the seabed would not be a discharge and would not require CWA NPDES permit authorization to add pollutants to those waters.

items.title: Process for Authorizing Seasonal Migratory Game Bird Hunting
items.content_text: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service or we) is changing the administrative process for authorizing seasonal migratory game bird hunting in the United States. Migratory game bird hunting regulations are currently promulgated annually to provide opportunities for recreation and sustenance; aid Federal, State, and Tribal governments in the management of migratory game birds; and allow harvests at levels compatible with migratory game bird population status and habitat conditions. The Service is adopting a more efficient administrative process for authorizing seasonal migratory game bird hunting. The Service will issue a memorandum to establish the limits and authorize seasonal migratory game bird hunting once every 3 years. The Service will continue to make annual decisions on harvest levels and will update the memorandum sooner than 3 years if changes are prescribed by our decision frameworks. The process eliminates the need for subsequent annual Federal regulation promulgation and rulemaking and is expected to increase efficiency; better meet State, Tribal, and Federal rulemaking constraints; and reduce the complexity and costs. Our goal is to better serve State partners and the hunting public while continuing to meet the legal and conservation purposes of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Tribes are already authorized under a similar process.

Judge Indira Talwani ruled yesterday that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in proving the administration’s order was unconstitutional. 

“Last night’s decision was wonderful news for Maine voters who rely on absentee voting,” Secretary Bellows said. “The judge made clear that the states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections. That goes to the heart of our legal fights in court against the Trump Administration. We will continue to stand with other states and voting rights advocates across the nation to defend the voting rights – including the right to vote by mail – for every citizen.”

In the decision, Judge Talwani wrote, “the Constitution charges the States with election administration” going on to say that no law has been passed by Congress that “would permit the USPS to regulate election mail.” The judge went even further to note that with just two months to the election, it would an expensive and likely impossible task for the 2026 election, saying, “Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible.”
